idiom_name: PyJWT: jwt.encode(claims, key, algorithm=...) and jwt.decode(..., algorithms=[...], audience=..., issuer=...)
implementation_notes: PyJWT is the realization: a dict (or a dataclass mapped to one) is the claim set, jwt.encode(claims, private_key, algorithm="RS256", headers={"kid": kid}) serializes and signs, and jwt.decode(token, public_key, algorithms=["RS256"], audience=..., issuer=...) is the consumer contract because PyJWT validates the signature and registered time and audience claims in one call. RSA, ECDSA, PS and EdDSA signing use the optional cryptography package; the PyJWT HS256 path does not need that extra package, but a production wrapper still owns algorithm pinning, key custody and mandatory claims. What replaces the classic structure: a dict plus one function call replaces the claim-assembly and signer classes, and the function or dataclass you keep owns the issuer, TTL, audience and replay identifier.
code_sketch:
import time
from uuid import uuid4
import jwt  # PyJWT
issued_at = int(time.time())
claims = {
    "iss": "https://idp.example",
    "sub": user_id,
    "aud": "https://api.example",
    "iat": issued_at,
    "exp": issued_at + 300,
    "jti": str(uuid4()),
}
token = jwt.encode(claims, private_key, algorithm="RS256", headers={"kid": kid})
# consumer: jwt.decode(token, public_key, algorithms=["RS256"],
#                      audience="https://api.example", issuer="https://idp.example")
pitfalls: jwt.decode requires an explicit algorithms list and refuses to infer it; never build that list from the token's own header, which is the algorithm-confusion bypass.
Passing a raw secret where an RSA key belongs (or the reverse) is the classic confusion hole; let PyJWT's key-type checks run instead of wrapping keys as bytes to silence them.
PyJWT converts datetime values for exp/iat/nbf into POSIX timestamps, so mixing datetimes and ints computed from different clocks silently shifts the validity window - keep one source of 'now'.
EdDSA and the asymmetric algorithms need the optional cryptography dependency; discovering that only in production usually means the fallback path signs with HS256 instead.
